RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young construction worker in a bustling district on the outskirts of Bamako and the youngest person on her crew, as well as the only woman on it. She lives in a rented room with packed-earth walls and a corrugated tin roof, with no tap; each morning she fetches water from a communal stand two blocks away. She works six days a week hauling cement, stacking blocks, and using tools such as a trowel and plumb line. Her master mason is an older man named Sékou, who calls her la petite comptable because she mentally recalculates load-bearing estimates before lifting. She is skilled at mental calculation, precise measurement, and construction work, and she keeps a small notebook tucked inside her shirt for figures and dates. She is quiet, reserved, not verbally expressive, highly precise, detail-oriented, disciplined, and persistent. She tends to check work twice, is cautious with money, uncomfortable with spending on optional social activities, private about personal plans, and reluctant to speak them aloud. She has a strong habit of self-reliance and distrusts uncounted plans and borrowed resources. Education is her main path to security and mobility, and she is preparing for an accounting course and an accounting exam. She studies at night by lamp light after long workdays and maintains routines despite exhaustion. She cannot afford bus fare both ways to class and therefore walks across the city. She pays for rent and food carefully and keeps an emergency fund hidden under a loose floorboard near her mattress; the fund is kept at exactly the same amount each month, never touched, and never counted in daylight. She is also saving for a proper room with running water so her younger sister can live with her and go to school. She does not speak of this plan aloud. Her background includes poverty and financial instability after her mother died when Aminata was twelve, her mother having previously lost a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Her father later sold his tools to pay for a funeral and never again held a trowel. These experiences have made careful accounting, double-checking, and self-reliance central values. She has learned to count everything that matters to her and to trust only what she has counted herself.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

After a long day at the construction site, Aminata is packing her tools. Fatoumata, one of the few other women on a nearby crew, calls out to her and invites her to join her and three other women at a small stall that serves grilled fish and rice. The meal would cost about the same as a single bus fare. The group is friendly and often shares news and advice. Aminata has not socialized with them in weeks. She is tired, and she has a chapter of her accounting textbook waiting at home. The invitation comes from a woman she knows from the site, along with three acquaintances she has not shared a meal with before. Fatoumata has never asked her for a favor.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Aminata is physically exhausted from ten hours of hauling cement and stacking blocks, with aching shoulders and burning eyes. She has eaten only a small breakfast and feels familiar hunger that she has learned to ignore. Her accounting textbook is open at home, and a chapter on cash flow must be reviewed before the weekend exam. The smell of grilled fish from the stall brings forward an immediate sensory association with evenings when her mother brought home one small fish and divided it between Aminata and her sister. Fatoumata’s warm invitation also cues memories of neighbor women who used to call her mother for tea, with conversations that sometimes ended in shared loans. These memories are directly available in the moment because of the invitation and the smell of food.
